posts.title: The Puppeteer setup that will capture trading heatmaps automatically
posts.body:
I'm building a system to capture dealer positioning data automatically.

The challenge: Skylit.ai requires login and has dynamic content.

The solution: Puppeteer with session management.

The architecture I'm building:

1. Authentication handling

Puppeteer launches Chrome with saved session.
Cookies persist login state.
No need to re-authenticate each capture.

2. Watchlist navigation

Dropdown: 'All Tickers' or custom list.
Arrow buttons: Cycle through tickers.
Automated via CSS selectors.

3. Screenshot scheduling

Capture schedule per ticker per day:
- First 30 min: Every 5 minutes (7 captures)
- 10:30 AM: 1 capture
- Midday: 1 capture
- Last 30 min: Every 5 minutes (7 captures)

~16 screenshots per ticker.

4. OCR extraction

Tesseract reads GEX/VEX values from images.
Structured data extracted from visual content.

5. Database storage

SQLite stores:
- Ticker and timestamp
- Screenshot path
- Extracted GEX/VEX values
- Associated technical data

Key technical decisions:

- Puppeteer over Playwright (better community support)
- Tesseract over cloud OCR (free, local)
- SQLite over Postgres (simpler for MVP)
- Node.js for Puppeteer, Python for analysis

Challenges to solve:

- Session persistence across restarts
- Handling page load delays
- OCR accuracy on heatmap colors
- Coordinating with market hours

Takeaway: Browser automation isn't just for testing. It's for building data collection systems from any web application.

posts.title: I built a Python file server for my project dashboard. Here's how.
tweets:
I built a Python file server for my project dashboard.

Secure file access from a web UI.

Here's how I did it:

The need:

My dashboard shows 39 projects.

I wanted to load real TODO.md and CLAUDE.md files when clicking a project.

But browsers can't access local files directly.

The solution: Python HTTP server.

Endpoints:
- /read-file → Read file contents
- /list-files → List directory contents

Security: Directory restriction

Server ONLY serves files from claudec directory.

Attempts to access other paths = 403 Forbidden.

# Validate path
if not resolved_path.startswith(BASE_DIR):
    return 403

The /read-file endpoint:

Input: file_path parameter
Output: File contents as text

Usage:
GET /read-file?path=/project/TODO.md

The /list-files endpoint:

Input: directory path
Output: JSON array of files with metadata

[
  {"name": "TODO.md", "size": 1024, "modified": "2025-01-29"},
  ...
]

Running the server:

python file-server.py
# Starts on port 8080

Dashboard makes fetch() calls to these endpoints.

Takeaway: When you need file access from a web UI, build a simple API server.

Python makes it easy. Keep security in mind (path validation).

posts.title: How I'm using OCR to extract data from trading heatmaps
posts.body:
The data I need: GEX and VEX values from Skylit.ai heatmaps.

The problem: These are images, not structured data.

The solution: OCR extraction.

The tool: Tesseract

Open-source OCR engine.
Free. Local. No API costs.

How it will work:

1. Capture heatmap screenshot

Puppeteer takes screenshot at scheduled times.
Saved as PNG with metadata.

2. Pre-process image

Crop to relevant region.
Adjust contrast for better OCR.
Convert to grayscale if needed.

3. Run OCR

import pytesseract
from PIL import Image

text = pytesseract.image_to_string(Image.open('heatmap.png'))

4. Parse extracted text

Find GEX/VEX patterns.
Extract numerical values.
Handle OCR errors.

5. Validate and store

Sanity check values.
Store with timestamp and ticker.

Challenges I'm anticipating:

- Color-on-color text (low contrast)
- Small font sizes
- Variable positioning
- OCR accuracy on numbers

Solutions I'm planning:

- Image pre-processing (contrast, crop)
- Multiple OCR passes
- Regex pattern matching
- Confidence scoring

Why not use an API?

- Cost: Cloud OCR charges per image
- Privacy: Data stays local
- Speed: No network latency
- Control: Full customization

Takeaway: OCR turns image data into structured data. Tesseract is free and good enough for most use cases.

posts.title: How webhooks automate my Twitter data collection
posts.body:
The old way: Polling.

- Check Apify every 5 minutes
- 'Is my job done yet?'
- Waste of API calls
- Delays in processing

The new way: Webhooks.

How it works:

1. Start Apify job

POST /api/twitter/collect
{
  "account": "@target_account",
  "webhook_url": "https://myserver.com/apify-webhook"
}

2. Apify runs the job

Scrapes Twitter data.
Processes in their cloud.
Takes a few minutes.

3. Apify calls my webhook

When done, Apify POSTs results to my endpoint.

POST /apify-webhook
{
  "status": "succeeded",
  "data": [...tweets...]
}

4. My server processes results

Parse the payload.
Store tweets in database.
Update job status.

No polling. No waiting. Instant processing.

The endpoint implementation:

@app.route('/apify-webhook', methods=['POST'])
def handle_apify_webhook():
    data = request.json
    if data['status'] == 'succeeded':
        tweets = data['data']
        for tweet in tweets:
            db.add_twitter_post(tweet)
        db.update_apify_job_status(data['job_id'], 'completed')
    return {'received': True}

Benefits over polling:

- Instant processing (no delay)
- No wasted API calls
- Cleaner code
- Better reliability

Takeaway: Webhooks > polling. Always. If the service supports webhooks, use them.

posts.title: How I process 2-hour X Spaces recordings automatically
posts.body:
The input: X Spaces URL.

The output: Audio file + transcript + AI summary.

The pipeline:

1. Download with yt-dlp

yt-dlp has built-in Twitter/X support.
Handles authentication via browser cookies.

yt-dlp 'https://x.com/i/spaces/...' -o 'audio.mp3'

2. Check file size

Whisper API limit: 25MB.
X Spaces recordings: Often 100MB+.

if file_size > 25MB:
    split_into_chunks()

3. Split with ffmpeg

ffmpeg -i audio.mp3 -f segment -segment_time 600 -c copy chunk_%03d.mp3

10-minute chunks. Clean splits.

4. Transcribe each chunk

Send to Whisper API.
Receive timestamped transcript.

for chunk in chunks:
    transcript = whisper.transcribe(chunk)
    all_transcripts.append(transcript)

5. Combine transcripts

Merge all chunks.
Adjust timestamps for continuity.

6. Generate summary

Send full transcript to GPT-4o or Gemini.

Prompt:
'Summarize this X Space. Include:
- Key insights
- Takeaways
- Advice
- Detailed overview'

7. Save outputs

- audio.mp3 (original recording)
- transcript.txt (timestamped text)
- summary.md (AI summary)

The command:

python spaces_pipeline.py 'https://x.com/i/spaces/...' --api-key 'xxx'

Takeaway: Long audio processing = chunking + combining. The pipeline handles files of any length.

posts.title: Why I run AI locally instead of using APIs.
tweets:
Why I run AI locally instead of using APIs.

Not always. But for many use cases.

Here's my reasoning:

Reason 1: Cost

APIs charge per token/request.

Local AI: One-time setup. Unlimited usage.

For high-volume tasks, local wins.

Reason 2: Privacy

API calls send your data to third parties.

Local AI: Data never leaves your machine.

For sensitive content, local wins.

Reason 3: No rate limits

APIs throttle heavy usage.
'Too many requests. Try again later.'

Local AI: Go as fast as your hardware allows.

Reason 4: Availability

APIs can have outages.
APIs can deprecate endpoints.
APIs can change pricing.

Local AI: Always available. Fully controlled.

The tradeoffs:

- Speed: APIs are faster (powerful servers)
- Quality: Top APIs (GPT-4) may be better than local models
- Setup: APIs are easier to start with
- Hardware: Local needs decent GPU for large models

My hybrid approach:

- Prototyping: Local (free experimentation)
- High volume: Local (no per-query cost)
- Speed-critical: API (faster responses)
- Production: Evaluate both

What I run locally:

- Ollama for chat (llama3.2)
- Whisper for transcription
- ChromaDB for vectors
- Embeddings (nomic-embed-text)

Takeaway: Local AI is viable for many use cases.

It's slower. But it's free and private.

Match the solution to the requirements.

posts.title: How I handle corrupted audio files in my transcription pipeline.
tweets:
How I handle corrupted audio files in my transcription pipeline.

X Spaces recordings can be messy.

Here's my error handling approach:

The problem:

X Spaces audio sometimes has:
- Missing MP3 frame headers
- Encoding issues
- Truncated data

pydub crashes on corrupted files.

Solution 1: Use ffmpeg directly

ffmpeg is more robust than Python libraries.

It can often process files that pydub can't.

Solution 2: Chunking by time, not size

Instead of splitting by file size, split by duration.

ffmpeg -i audio.mp3 -f segment -segment_time 600 ...

10-minute chunks regardless of file issues.

Solution 4: Progress saving

Save state after each successful chunk.

If failure occurs, resume from last checkpoint.

No re-processing successful chunks.

Solution 5: Graceful degradation

If one chunk fails, continue with others.

Partial transcript > no transcript.

Flag missing sections for review.

The resilient pipeline:

1. Try normal processing
2. On failure, try ffmpeg repair
3. On failure, try chunking
4. On failure, log and continue
5. Always save progress

Takeaway: Audio pipelines need error handling.

Corrupted files are common.

Build resilient systems that degrade gracefully.

posts.title: Why every data pipeline I build has checkpointing.
tweets:
Why every data pipeline I build has checkpointing.

Lesson learned: Jobs fail. Networks timeout. APIs rate limit.

Checkpointing saves you.

What is checkpointing?

Saving progress at regular intervals.

If job fails at record 500, restart from 500.

Not from 0.

The resume logic:

def resume_from_checkpoint():
    checkpoint = load_checkpoint()
    start_from = checkpoint['last_processed'] + 1
    return records[start_from:]

Real example from OwnerScraper:

103 CDL schools to enrich.

Save every 5 schools.

If Perplexity API rate limits at school 50:
- Restart from school 46
- Not from school 1

Why this matters:

- API rate limits: Common
- Network issues: Common
- Process crashes: Common

Without checkpointing: Lose all progress.
With checkpointing: Lose 5-10 records max.

Takeaway: Always build checkpointing into data pipelines.

The extra 10 lines of code save hours of re-processing.

posts.title: The setup scoring algorithm I'm building for Heatseeker
posts.body:
Goal: Score trading setups objectively.

Not gut feel. Not FOMO. Algorithm.

The scoring dimensions:

1. Heatseeker signal quality (40%)

- First touch vs retested node
- Node growing vs unwinding
- Gatekeeper vs King node
- Color/magnitude alignment

2. Technical confirmation (30%)

- Price at support/resistance
- EMA alignment
- Volume confirmation
- Candle patterns

3. Multi-index confluence (20%)

- SPX alignment
- SPY alignment
- QQQ alignment
- Sector ETF alignment

4. Risk/reward (10%)

- Asymmetric R:R (> 1.5:1)
- Clear stop level
- Realistic target

The scoring logic:

def score_setup(heatseeker_data, technical_data, index_data):
    score = 0
    
    # Heatseeker signals
    if is_first_touch(heatseeker_data):
        score += 15
    if is_growing_node(heatseeker_data):
        score += 15
    if is_gatekeeper_rejection(heatseeker_data):
        score += 10
    
    # Technical confirmation
    if at_support_resistance(technical_data):
        score += 10
    if ema_aligned(technical_data):
        score += 10
    if volume_confirms(technical_data):
        score += 10
    
    # Index confluence
    aligned_indices = count_aligned_indices(index_data)
    score += aligned_indices * 5  # 5 points per aligned index
    
    # Risk/reward
    if rr_ratio(technical_data) > 1.5:
        score += 10
    
    return score / 100  # Normalize to 0-10

Alert threshold: ≥ 7/10

Below 7: Skip.
Above 7: Alert for review.

Takeaway: Systematize trading decisions. Algorithms don't have FOMO. Algorithms follow rules.

posts.title: My fully local AI stack: $0/month, unlimited usage.
tweets:
My fully local AI stack: $0/month, unlimited usage.

No APIs. No rate limits. No costs.

Here's what I run:

LLM: Ollama + llama3.2

Ollama is a local LLM runtime.
llama3.2 is a capable open-source model.

Install: brew install ollama
Run: ollama pull llama3.2

Embeddings: nomic-embed-text

Converts text to vectors for similarity search.

Also via Ollama:
ollama pull nomic-embed-text

Vector database: ChromaDB

Stores and searches embeddings.

Fully local. File-based.

pip install chromadb

Transcription: Whisper

OpenAI's speech-to-text model.
Runs locally on your machine.

pip install openai-whisper

RAG framework: LangChain

Connects all the pieces.

Document loading → chunking → embedding → retrieval → generation

The stack in action (YouTubeRAG):

1. Fetch YouTube transcripts
2. Chunk into pieces
3. Embed with nomic-embed-text
4. Store in ChromaDB
5. Query with llama3.2
6. Get answers

Performance tradeoffs:

Local is slower (30 sec vs 3 sec).
But: unlimited usage, no costs, full privacy.

When I use local vs API:

- Prototyping: Local
- High volume: Local
- Speed-critical: API
- Privacy-sensitive: Local

Takeaway: You can run capable AI locally.

It's slower. But it's free and private.

For many use cases, that's the right choice.
